title: The offering and the jackal
hookLine: Andal calls herself an offering already set before the Lord; why food for God is offered before anyone tastes it
carry: what's offered to god is set apart
last: THE GUEST IS TREATED AS GOD.

cards: An offering is laid out for the gods. Priests have prepared it with care, by the rules, for the sacred fire. Then a jackal slips in from the forest and sniffs at it.

Ruined. Nobody could offer it now. That rough little picture comes from a young woman's poem, and she's using it about herself: what would happen to her if anyone so much as talked of marrying her to a man.
The woman is Andal, and today she speaks for herself.

teach.b: Year three met Andal in the Tiruppavai, one cowherd girl among many. Her other work, the Nachiyar Tirumoli, the sacred words of the lady, is her own voice. Take the jackal verse, in paraphrase.

My heart is set on the Lord who holds the conch and the wheel. If anyone speaks of giving me to a mortal man, I won't live. It would be like the offering made for the gods being sniffed by a jackal of the forest.
She doesn't say marriage is bad. She borrows a picture every Hindu kitchen knows.

teach.h: FOOD FOR GOD IS SET APART
teach.b: Food made for God is set apart.

teach.h: PRASAD: IT COMES BACK AS A GIFT
teach.b: In many homes no one tastes it first; it's placed before the Lord, and only then does it come back to the family as prasad, a blessed gift. Andal says she is that food, already offered. Now notice whom she asks for help.
The same book opens with her pleading with Kama, the god of desire, sweeping the ground and drawing in the sand for him, asking him to join her to the Lord.

Sri Vaishnava teachers have a word for giving yourself wholly to God: sharanagati, taking refuge, surrender. Many of them read Andal's longing as the soul's own, belonging to the Lord before it belongs to anyone.
Other readers also hear a young woman saying whom she will and won't belong to. The tradition never had to pick one. It counts her among the Alvars, the poet-saints, and keeps singing her verses.

how: Sri Vaishnava Hindus honor Andal as one of the Alvars and recite her Tiruppavai and Nachiyar Tirumoli in temples and homes; in many Hindu homes, food is offered to God before anyone eats, and comes back as prasad.

o: a temple dancer who sang for the king at dawn
a queen who gave her jewels to a Vishnu temple
a poet-saint whose heart was set on the Lord alone

games.q: the offering and the jackal — tap the pairs.
p: sniffs the offering meant for the gods
food offered to God, given back as a gift

s: in many Hindu homes, food cooked for the offering is tasted first to check it
it's set apart and offered to God first. then it comes back to the family as prasad.
in the jackal verse, Andal says marriage itself is bad
she says she's already promised to the Lord, so any other match would spoil the offering.
Andal asks Kama, the god of desire, to join her to the Lord
the poem opens with her drawing in the sand and pleading with him.

games.q: you're Andal. your heart is set on the Lord, and you want help getting there. whom do you turn to first in the poem?
games.why: she sweeps the ground, draws in the sand, and pleads with Kama to join her to the Lord: ordinary love's god, asked to lead her past an ordinary match.

practice: Before your next meal or drink today, pause with it in front of you. Many Hindus offer their food to God first, silently or with a short prayer, before the first bite, so the meal comes back to them as prasad.
Try it now, even with a glass of water: one breath, set it before God, then drink. If you don't pray, let the pause be simple thanks for what's in front of you.
